540.title: While the mind still works
540.hook: hurry, not only because death nears, but because understanding may fail first (Meditations 3.1)
540.howItsDone: Some readers take this entry as a push to stop postponing tasks that need clear thinking, such as important letters, plans and conversations with older relatives.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of book two, life as a stranger's sojourn. Your line was a traveler's stay. What did you treat as borrowed, and care for? Day five hundred forty.

Watching a grandparent slowly lose their memory can bring a particular kind of sadness. The body is still here. The hands, the laugh, the way they hold a cup. But the person who could tell you the story, or give you the advice, or say the thing you were waiting to hear, is harder and harder to reach. Book three opens with a short note in the manuscripts, at Carnuntum, a fortress on the Danube. Then Marcus looks straight at that possibility for himself. This is a tender one. Today: while the mind still works.
screen: `THE BODY STILL HERE.` → `THE PERSON HARDER TO REACH.` → `WHILE THE MIND STILL WORKS.`

segments.voice: First, the usual reminder. Each day, Marcus says, life is spent, and less of it remains. We've heard that from him and from Seneca before. Second, the new worry. But there's something else to consider, he says. Even if a person lives longer, it isn't certain that the mind will stay able to understand things, to think about what's human and what's divine. Breathing, eating, imagining, wanting: those may carry on. What can go first is the power to use ourselves well: to see our duties clearly, to sort out appearances, to think something through. Third, so hurry. Therefore, he says, we must hurry. Not only because death comes closer every day, but because understanding may stop before life does. Fourth, how to hear that kindly. This isn't a judgment on anyone whose mind has changed with age or illness. A person's worth doesn't leave with their memory, and the people who care for them know it. Marcus is talking to himself, about timing. If there's something that needs a clear mind, don't assume the clear mind will always be there. The letter to your children. The hard conversation. The will. The forgiveness. Learning the thing you keep saying you'll learn. Even the conversations with the older people you love, while they can still tell you the story. Notice the shape of the urgency. It isn't panic. It's the same steady push we've met all year: today, not someday. Marcus adds one more reason to it. Not only while I live. While I can.
screen: `EACH DAY, LESS REMAINS.` · `THE MIND MAY GO FIRST.` · `SO HURRY.` · `WHAT NEEDS A CLEAR MIND, DO NOW.` · then, large: `WHILE I CAN.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Notice that your mind is working right now: following words, holding a thought, choosing where to rest. Let that be a small wonder for a moment. Then think of one thing that needs this clear mind, something you've been putting off. A letter. A decision. A question for an older relative. Picture doing it this week, while you can. The bell holds the time.
While the mind still works. Marcus says hurry, not only because death nears, but because understanding may fail before life does. Today's word.

541.title: Answer openly
541.hook: think only thoughts you could say out loud if suddenly asked (Meditations 3.4)
541.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism use Marcus's test during the day, asking whether their current thought is one they could say out loud without embarrassment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: while the mind still works, and the things that need it. Your line was while I can. What did you stop saving for later? Day five hundred forty-one.

Penny for your thoughts. Someone says it across the table, and for a split second there can be a small panic. Because the honest answer might be: I was replaying that argument and winning it this time. Or: I was comparing my life to my cousin's. Or: I was wondering what those two are whispering about. So we say, oh, nothing. Marcus turns that little moment into a test. Not for what you say. For what you think. Today: answer openly.

First, where thoughts go. Section four begins with a warning. Don't waste what's left of your life, Marcus says, thinking about other people, unless it's for some common good: what so-and-so is doing and why, what they're saying, what they're scheming. All of that pulls you away from watching your own ruling part. Last week he warned against prying into other people's souls. Here, it's how much of our own quiet thinking drifts to them. Second, the test. Get used to thinking only the kind of thoughts that, if someone suddenly asked, what are you thinking about right now, you could answer at once, openly: this, or that. Third, what passes. If you could answer like that, he says, it would be plain that everything in you is simple and kind, fit for a person who lives among others. No thought of pleasure or indulgence, no rivalry, no envy, no suspicion, nothing you'd blush to admit you were thinking. It's a high bar. Notice his verb: get used to it. A habit, built slowly. Fourth, the person who passes. Someone like that, he says, is like a priest and servant of the gods, at home with the divine within, untouched by pleasure, unhurt by pain, wrestling in the noblest contest, not to be overthrown by any passion. Readers on different paths hear that differently; Marcus meant the spirit within he's been tending all through book two. The test itself is simple enough for anyone. Not a vow of perfect thoughts. Just a question to carry, and to ask before a thought settles in: could I say it?

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let your thoughts come and go for a moment. Then imagine someone kind, sitting across from you, asking gently: what are you thinking right now? Notice your answer. Could you say it out loud? If yes, fine. If not, don't scold yourself. Just ask what the thought needs: to be let go, or turned into something you could say. Check one more thought the same way. The bell holds the time.
Answer openly. Marcus: think only thoughts you could say out loud at once if someone suddenly asked, nothing you'd blush to admit. Today's word.
Your line: could I say it. Three times today, ask what you're thinking right now, and whether you could say it openly. Day five hundred forty-one.

542.title: If you find anything better
542.hook: if you find anything better than justice, truth, self-control and courage, turn to it; if not, make room for nothing else (Meditations 3.6)
542.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use the four virtues of Meditations 3.6 as an evening check: was I just, truthful, self-controlled and brave today?

segments.voice: Yesterday: answer openly. Your line was could I say it. Was there a thought you caught that you'd rather nobody heard, and what did you do with it? Day five hundred forty-two.

Most advice tells you what to want. Marcus Aurelius, in the sixth entry of his third book, does something stranger. He issues a challenge, and it's aimed at himself. Go ahead, he says. Search all of human life. If you find something better than the four things I'm about to name, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy it. He isn't defending a position. He's daring himself to beat it. An emperor who could have anything is asking what's actually worth having. Today: if you find anything better.
screen: `A CHALLENGE, AIMED AT HIMSELF.` → `SEARCH ALL OF HUMAN LIFE.` → `IF YOU FIND ANYTHING BETTER.`

segments.voice: First, the four. Marcus names them: justice, truth, self-control and courage. Readers of Plato will hear the old Greek list of four virtues, where wisdom usually stands. Marcus puts truth in that place, which tells you something about him. For a man surrounded by flatterers, truth was a daily discipline. Second, the dare. If you find anything better than these, he says, turn to it. And he raises the stakes: if you find anything better than the guiding spirit inside you, the reason that governs your choices and keeps you honest, take that instead. Then he answers his own dare. If nothing better turns up, and he expects nothing will, then make room for nothing else. Third, the rivals. Marcus names what usually crowds in: praise from the crowd, power, wealth, the enjoyment of pleasures. He doesn't call them evil. His worry is subtler. Let one of them sit beside the four as an equal, even for a little while, and it starts to take over without asking. A second loyalty quietly becomes the first. Fourth, choose simply. Simply and freely choose the better, he writes, and hold on to it. Not a long calculation every morning, weighing virtue against convenience. One choice, made plainly, then kept. Here's what makes this useful on an ordinary Tuesday. You can test your own day against the list. Was I fair? Was I true? Did I hold back where I needed to? Did I do the hard thing? Four questions, and the dare stays open.
screen: `THE FOUR: JUSTICE, TRUTH, CONTROL, COURAGE.` · `THE DARE: FIND SOMETHING BETTER.` · `THE RIVALS: PRAISE, POWER, WEALTH.` · `CHOOSE SIMPLY, AND HOLD ON.` · then, large: `NOTHING BETTER.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Walk back through your day so far, or yesterday if it's early. Find one moment for each of the four. Justice: when did you treat someone fairly, or not? Truth: when did you say what was so? Self-control: when did you hold back? Courage: when did you do the uncomfortable thing? Don't grade too hard. Just notice which of the four got the most room today, and which got crowded out. The bell holds the time.
Self-control. One of the four goods in Marcus's dare, alongside justice, truth and courage: if you find anything better, turn to it. If not, give room to nothing else. Today's word.
Your line: nothing better. When praise, money or comfort pulls at you today, ask whether it's really better than the four. Then choose simply. Day five hundred forty-two.

543.title: Never break faith
543.hook: value nothing that makes you break your word or lose self-respect (Meditations 3.7)
543.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius treat Meditations 3.7 as a household test: if a desire only works in hiding, behind walls and curtains, they count it as a loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday: self-control, one of the four goods to turn to. Your line was nothing better. Which of the four, justice, truth, self-control or courage, got crowded out of your day? Day five hundred forty-three.

Curtains can tell you something about a house. Some hang there for warmth, or for sleep. And sometimes a curtain is there for another reason: the purchase nobody mentioned, the deleted message, the plan someone would rather nobody saw. Marcus Aurelius used curtains as a test. In the seventh entry of his third book, he lists the things a person should never count as worth having, and he ends the list with an image of walls and curtains. Today: never break faith.
screen: `CURTAINS ON A HOUSE.` → `WHAT NEEDS CURTAINS?` → `NEVER BREAK FAITH.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. Never value anything as good for you, Marcus writes, if it will one day force you to break your word or lose your self-respect. Notice the order. He doesn't start with what's forbidden. He starts with what we value. If a thing would cost you your word, it was never really a gain. Second, the longer list. He goes on: nothing that makes you hate anyone, suspect anyone, curse anyone, play the hypocrite. Each one is a small way of breaking faith, with another person or with yourself. Third, walls and curtains. The list ends with anything you'd want that needs walls and curtains around it. It's a plain household test. If a desire only works in hiding, Marcus counts it as a loss, however good it looks. It connects to the line from two days ago: think only what you could say out loud. Fourth, the person who keeps faith. Marcus describes them. They put their own mind and its goodness first. They don't make a tragedy of things, don't groan, don't need either solitude or a crowd. They don't chase life and they don't run from it. Here's the useful part for an ordinary day. Breaking faith is rarely one big betrayal. It's usually small: the call you said you'd make, the favor you said you'd do, the time you said you'd be there. A small promise kept is still a promise kept, and a word that holds in small things is easier to trust in large ones. That's what Marcus is protecting: not a reputation, but a self you can respect.

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one promise you've made that's still open. It can be tiny: I'll call you back, I'll send that, I'll be there at six. Picture the person who heard you say it. Now picture keeping it today, plainly, without fuss. Decide when. Then let the breath carry a quiet sense of what it's like to be someone whose word holds. The bell holds the time.
Marcus, whose rule was to value nothing that would cost your word, your self-respect, or something that needs walls and curtains. Today's word.
Your line: keep faith. Keep one promise today, even a small one, and keep it on time. Day five hundred forty-three.

544.title: Honor the power of judgment
544.hook: revere your capacity to form opinions; it keeps you free (Meditations 3.9)
544.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius practice Meditations 3.9 by pausing between an event and their verdict about it, separating what they saw from what they added.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Marcus's rule against broken promises. Your line was keep faith. Which promise did you keep, and was it on time? Day five hundred forty-four.

Count the opinions you've formed today. The coffee is weak. That driver is a jerk. My boss is annoyed with me. This headline is outrageous. That person on the train looks unfriendly. Opinions like these can pile up before lunch, fast and unnoticed. They can feel like seeing, not like deciding. Marcus Aurelius had a name for the quiet machine that turns what happens into what we think about it. He didn't just tell himself to use it. He told himself to revere it. Today: honor the power of judgment.
screen: `OPINIONS BEFORE LUNCH.` → `THEY CAN FEEL LIKE SEEING.` → `HONOR THE POWER OF JUDGMENT.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In the ninth entry of book three Marcus tells himself to revere the faculty that forms opinions. The Greek word means supposing, taking a thing to be so. In the Stoic picture, before you act, before you feel, you've already judged. That judging is the hinge. Second, everything depends on it. Marcus says this power is what keeps your mind from holding any opinion that goes against nature and against what a reasoning creature is meant to be. If it's careless, everything downstream is careless: the anger, the fear, the reply you send. If it's careful, the rest has a chance. Third, what it promises. Marcus lists three gifts from a well-kept judgment. Freedom from hasty conclusions. Friendliness toward other people. And following the gods, which for a Stoic meant living in step with the order of things. Notice the second one. Marcus ties careful judgment to friendliness, and it isn't hard to see why: unkindness often rests on a quick verdict about someone we barely know. Fourth, why it keeps you free. This is the Stoic thread we've been following since Epictetus: you can't control what happens, but you can control what you take it to mean. A prisoner, a slave, an emperor, each has this power. No one can form an opinion for you unless you let them. Here's the Tuesday version. Between the event and your verdict there's a small gap. Revering judgment just means using the gap. Ask: is that what I saw, or what I decided?
screen: `REVERE THE FACULTY THAT FORMS OPINIONS.` · `EVERYTHING DOWNSTREAM DEPENDS ON IT.` · `NO HASTE, FRIENDLINESS, THE GODS.` · `NO ONE CAN JUDGE FOR YOU.` · then, large: `JUDGE CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Pick one opinion you formed quickly today, about a person or a situation. Say it to yourself in a sentence. Now slow it down. What did you actually see or hear? What did you add? Is there another story that fits the same facts? Then form one careful opinion in place of the quick one. It may be the same verdict. It may be softer. Either way, this time you chose it. The bell holds the time.
Marcus, who told himself to revere the faculty that forms opinions, since careful judgment guards against haste and makes room for friendliness. Today's word.
Your line: judge carefully. Once today, when a verdict about someone pops up, ask: is that what I saw, or what I decided? Day five hundred forty-four.

545.title: Only now
545.hook: each lives only this moment; the rest is gone or unknown (Meditations 3.10)
545.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius return to Meditations 3.10 when worry or regret pulls at them, bringing their attention back to the present moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Marcus on revering judgment. Your line was judge carefully. When a verdict popped up, did you catch the gap between what you saw and what you decided? Day five hundred forty-five.

Where are you right now? Not where your body is. Where your mind is. Maybe it's replaying a conversation from Tuesday, or rehearsing one for Friday. The past rides along like a backpack, the future hangs ahead like a weather forecast, and the one place we actually stand gets barely a glance. Marcus Aurelius set all of that down in a few short lines, in the tenth entry of his third book. Today: only now.
screen: `WHERE IS YOUR MIND?` → `TUESDAY BEHIND, FRIDAY AHEAD.` → `ONLY NOW.`

segments.voice: First, throw the rest away. Marcus opens the tenth entry of book three by telling himself to let everything else go and hold on to these few things. It's a clearing-out. Second, the moment. Each of us, he says, lives only the present, this moment that can't be divided. Everything else is either already lived or uncertain. That's not a mood. It's a description. You cannot live yesterday again, and you cannot yet live tomorrow. In his terms, the only life anyone actually has is happening in this breath. Third, how small it all is. Then Marcus widens the lens. Short is the life each person lives. Small is the corner of the earth where they live it. Short, too, is the longest fame after death, and it's passed along by people who will die soon themselves, who don't know even themselves, let alone someone long gone. He's not trying to depress himself. He's pulling his attention back from the places it wanders, the regrets and the legacy, to the one place it can do any good. Fourth, why this is freedom. If the past is finished and the future unknown, then neither one is where your choices happen. The present is small, but it's the only part of life you can steer. Other contemplative traditions have their own words for returning to this moment. For Marcus, it's plain arithmetic. As he put it back in book two, the present is the only thing anyone can lose, because it's the only thing anyone has.

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Feel this breath: the cool air coming in, the slight warmth going out. That's it. That's the whole of your life right now. When your mind drifts to earlier today, notice it, and say quietly, gone. When it drifts to later, notice it, and say, unknown. Then come back to this breath. And this one. Only this. The bell holds the time.
Only now. Marcus says each person lives only this moment; the past is already lived, and the future is uncertain. Today's word.
Your line: only this. Three times today, when your mind runs ahead or behind, feel one breath and say: only this. Day five hundred forty-five.

546.title: Define it
546.hook: describe each thing plainly, stripped bare, as it is (Meditations 3.11)
546.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius practice Meditations 3.11 by writing a worry down in one plain sentence, naming what it is and what it asks of them, before deciding how to respond.

segments.voice: Yesterday: only now. Your line was only this. When your mind ran ahead or behind, did one breath bring it back? Day five hundred forty-six, the end of a week.

A worry rarely arrives in plain words. It arrives as a cloud. Something about money. Something about that test result. Something about the way she said goodnight. It's big and blurry and it fills the room. Now try to write it down in one flat sentence, the way a clerk would. Sometimes the cloud shrinks the moment it has edges. Marcus Aurelius used this trick on himself, and wrote down exactly how it works. Today: define it.
screen: `A WORRY ARRIVES AS A CLOUD.` → `WRITE IT LIKE A CLERK.` → `DEFINE IT.`

segments.voice: First, the method. The eleventh entry of book three opens by calling this one more aid to add to the others. Marcus writes: always make a definition, or a description, of whatever presents itself to your mind. See what it is in its substance, stripped bare, whole, and tell yourself its name, and the names of the parts it's made of. Second, why bare. Marcus's point is that what upsets us is often less the thing than the coat we put on it. A late bill becomes I'm failing at life. A curt email becomes they're about to fire me. Defining strips the coat off. A late bill is a piece of paper asking for an amount by a date. That may still be a problem, but now it's a problem you can see. Third, the questions. Marcus goes on to ask of each thing: what is it, what is it made of, how long will it last, and what does it ask of me? Gentleness, courage, truth, faithfulness, simplicity? A defined thing points to a response. A cloud just points to dread. He says nothing so enlarges the mind as being able to examine everything that happens methodically and truly. Fourth, the week. Look at what this week has built. While I can: the mind won't last forever. Could I say it: think only what you could say out loud. Nothing better: the four goods. Keep faith: your word. Judge carefully: the power that forms opinions. Only this: the present. And now, as it is. Seven short lines, each small enough to say in one breath.

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring up one worry that's been sitting with you. Let it be a cloud for a moment. Now describe it plainly, as a clerk would, in one flat sentence. No adjectives, no predictions. What is it, actually? What is it made of? How long will it last? Then ask Marcus's last question: what does it ask of me? Patience, a phone call, courage? Notice the size of it now. The bell holds the time.
Define it. Marcus's method: describe each thing plainly, stripped bare, name it and its parts, and ask what it asks of you. Today's word.
Your line: as it is. When something upsets you today, say it back to yourself in one flat sentence, as it is, before you react. Day five hundred forty-six.

fork.setup: on the drive to work, your car starts making a new grinding noise. your mind fills with storm clouds. what fits 3.11?
options: imagine every way it could go wrong.
describe it plainly: a new noise, from the front, when braking.
turn up the radio and ignore it.
fork.reveal: Marcus defines the thing bare: a noise, with a place and a time. what it asks of you, for now, is a call to a mechanic and some patience.

original.note: Greek, 'appearance, impression': in Stoic language, what presents itself to the mind before we judge it.

trapdoor: what you thought: be precise.
what it means: strip each thing to its bare substance, name its parts, and ask what it asks of you.
what a scholar hears: the Stoics worked with the phantasia, the impression; defining it plainly is how assent is kept honest.
